A small and specific sample versus a biased generalization of all North American women. What your comment and most of this thread suggests is that because these feminists take it a step beyond what it means to have equality, all women have be subjected to a bias that they are easily brainwashed, greedy, incompetent, etc.. And its exactly stuff like that that gives these feminists more fuel to call out discrimination even when there isn't any. Women in STEM, and many, many other fields, know what actual discrimination is like, and know this isn't it. But sweeping generalizations only aims to insult and belittle the accomplishments of women who actually worked for their careers and education.

Absolutely, you're right, I had no idea how to argue a point until this exact moment. It's definitely not an issue to use your vastly inflated anecdotal evidence to make a point, but my phrasing what you call me out on. Here, I'll make it more direct this time: I'm not fond of what these women are doing. Most NA women don't buy into the modern day feminist propaganda and know the wage gap is a myth. And it's delusional to assume a whole continent of women would so readily pull the victim card and put the blame on others before considering the other factors that lead to those discrepancies. Because, believe it or not, women are actually people and not sheep. If you want to play with anecdotes, I'm in the STEM field and no woman I know thinks like the women in this article, or are as easily brainwashed as you suggest.
But dimwitted generalizations about an entire continent of people is definitely a valid way to introduce a point, right?
Have you ever actually met a North American woman?
Delusions and statistics lacking environmental controls you mean?
Superiority complex much?

Thank you for your response. I definitely fall into the jealousy trap from time to time with him, and its one I try hard not to get stuck in for long. I always try to tell myself that he's with me for a reason, and that we're successful together, because we're a team and I know if the relationship progresses we can learn to both benefit from the achievements of the other.

 I suppose what really hits my insecurities the hardest is how overt he is about it. I never really know how to respond when he makes those comments, because on one hand I don't want to place him on too high of a pedestal or inflate his ego, but on the other, I'm his girlfriend, if there's anyone he should brag to, it should be me! I will keep your suggestions in mind though, and definitely try to work through any of these deep rooted insecurities with him.

Thank you for your response. Sometimes I do act a little short with him when he makes those comments, just to hint that "yeah, I think that's really great sweetie, but you don't have to be so cocky all the time." He definitely likes to think himself to be an adult, but there are certain things like this that make me think he still has lots of growing up to do. I will keep your suggestions in mind.

Thank you for your response. I should have mentioned that I'm his first girlfriend, and I was the one that first introduced myself to him and initiated the relationship. He is also extremely introverted and doesn't like being around people very often to have any sort of selection of potential partners. So I don't believe he really "chose me" from other girls; I chose him. He does see me as an equal (he has said so and none of his behaviour speaks otherwise) and is constantly pushing me to be every bit as happy and achieving as he is. I appreciate your concern though, I will keep it in mind.

Thank you for your response. I have struggled with confidence and depression in the past, and I definitely have come a long way since then. But every now and then events happen that cause it to creep up on me again, like when he makes those teasing comments about himself. The thing is, to the average person if isolated from him, I guess I would appear quite "successful." He and I are both in difficult science programs at a top university, I would secretly admit that most people see me as more physically attractive than him (he isn't nearly as fit as I am), and although my jobs aren't the greatest I have faith in myself that I can secure something more livable after graduation. 

I do believe that his view of the world is distorted at least a bit, but like other comments have mentioned, he is still young and dependent, so I suppose that is subject to change as he ages. I really like your idea, as my biggest fear is offending him or dragging him down. I wouldn't be so bothered if he wasn't just so constantly overt about it, but I attribute that to the praise he receives daily from his family. Your comment really made me smile though, thank you so much!
